To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
BGs from Escherichiacoli carrying ice nucleationprotein InaZ fromPseudomonassyringaein theiroutermembrane arefunctional ice nucleators.

BGs of recombinant E.coli carrying InaZ from Ps.syringae functionally display this protein on their surface and that these BGs are non-living cell envelopes retaining the ice-nucleating activity of the recombinant bacteria and no longer representing a GMO.
BGs from E. coli carrying ice nucleating protein InaZ can be used as a functional model system for the induction of heterogeneous ice formation.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of an alternative approach for the functional display of ice nucleating proteins on the surface of BGs, which may be used for a more environmentally friendly and sustainable ice nucleation technology.
a new type of ice nucleation particles, which are not only able to induce heterogeneous ice crystal formation but are also biologically inactive.
the development of new ice nucleation agents for applications such as the prevention of ice formation in the atmosphere or in industrial cooling systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the BGs are able to induce ice formation at temperatures below −7 °C, which is the lowest temperature that has ever been achieved by living recombinant bacteria carrying InaZ on its surface.
BGs from recombinant E.coli carrying InaZ are able to induce heterogeneous ice nucleation.
the BGs are not ice nucleation active.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
BGs are promising candidates for the functional display of InaZ. The results of this study are a first step towards the application of BGs as ice-nucleation agents in the food industry.
BGs from recombinant E.coli expressing the Pseudomonas ice nucleation protein are able to nucleate ice formation in ultra-pure water at temperatures below −6.7°C.
BGs are an attractive alternative to their living counterparts for functional surface display of InaZ and for the production of other proteins of interest.
The main takeaway from our work is that
BGs can be considered as a novel class of ice nucleators with a potential for applications in the field of biotechnology.
BGs are an alternative to living cells for the application of ice-nucleation proteins in biotechnological processes.
BGs carrying functional InaZ on its surface represent a new tool to induce ice formation at a given temperature.
